items.title: Saturdays 80s Jam – Right Here Waiting – Richard Marx
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Released in 1989, Richard Marx’s “Right Here Waiting” became one of the defining romantic ballads of the late 1980s. It was the kind of song that could turn a quiet moment into a full-blown emotional crisis, complete with longing, separation, and the promise that no matter how far away someone might be, one person would still be waiting.

The song came from a surprisingly personal place. Marx wrote it while his future wife, actress Cynthia Rhodes, was filming a movie in South Africa. The two were separated by thousands of miles, and Marx began writing a letter to her. Instead of finishing the letter, he turned his feelings into a song.

That personal origin is a big part of why “Right Here Waiting” feels so direct. There is no complicated story to follow. The song is essentially about missing someone so badly that distance becomes almost unbearable.

Marx recorded the song for his second studio album, , released in 1989. Although the album contained several more upbeat pop-rock songs, “Right Here Waiting” stood apart. Built around piano, keyboards, acoustic guitar, and Marx’s increasingly emotional vocal, it was deliberately simple compared with many of the huge productions dominating pop radio at the time.

Marx had already established himself as a successful singer and songwriter, but “Right Here Waiting” took his career to another level. The song became a massive international hit, reaching number one on the Billboard Hot 100 and topping charts in numerous countries.

It was also an enormous adult-contemporary success, fitting perfectly into the radio landscape of the late 1980s. At a time when power ballads were everywhere, Marx managed to make his version stand out by keeping the focus on the melody and emotion rather than overwhelming the song with production.

The lyrics were also unusually conversational for a major pop ballad. Marx wasn’t presenting some elaborate poetic fantasy. He was describing the frustration of being separated from someone he loved and the determination to remain emotionally connected despite the distance.

That made the song incredibly easy for listeners to adopt as their own.

It quickly became associated with long-distance relationships, breakups, weddings, slow dances, and just about any situation involving romantic longing. For an entire generation, “Right Here Waiting” became one of those songs that could instantly transport someone back to a particular relationship or moment.

Marx’s vocal performance is crucial to that effect. He doesn’t begin by throwing everything at the listener. Instead, the performance gradually builds, allowing the emotion to become more intense as the song progresses.

By the final chorus, the arrangement has expanded, but the central idea remains unchanged: distance may be painful, but the commitment remains.

The song also benefited from arriving at the perfect moment for the romantic ballad. The late 1980s were packed with enormous pop productions, but there was still a huge audience for songs that could work with nothing more than a singer, a melody, and a story.

“Right Here Waiting” proved that a ballad didn’t need elaborate tricks to become enormous.

More than three decades later, the song remains one of Richard Marx’s signature recordings. It helped establish him as one of the major adult-pop songwriters of his generation and became a permanent part of the late-1980s romantic soundtrack.

Its appeal is remarkably simple.

Someone you love is far away.

You don’t know exactly when you’ll be together again.

But you’re still waiting.

Sometimes the simplest idea is the one that connects with the most people, and “Right Here Waiting” turned that feeling into one of 1989’s most enduring pop songs.

items.title: Forgotten Band: Mudhoney
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There is something slightly ridiculous about calling Mudhoney a forgotten band.

They were there when the Seattle music scene was turning into the biggest rock story on the planet. They released records on Sub Pop. They helped establish the sound that would eventually be labeled grunge. Kurt Cobain was a fan. Their music became part of the soundtrack to one of the most important alternative-rock movements of the late 1980s and early 1990s.

And yet, when people talk about grunge today, Mudhoney often gets pushed several places down the list.

Everybody remembers Nirvana.

Everybody remembers Pearl Jam.

Soundgarden and Alice in Chains get their share of attention.

Then somebody mentions Mudhoney and you can practically see the question forming:

“Wait… weren’t they one of those Seattle bands?”

They were one of Seattle bands.

Except they were there before almost everybody else.

Before Grunge Was a Thing

Mudhoney formed in Seattle in 1988, emerging from the ashes of two hugely important underground bands: Green River and The Melvins-adjacent scene that was developing around the Pacific Northwest.

The original lineup featured Mark Arm on vocals, Steve Turner on guitar, Matt Lukin on bass and Dan Peters on drums.

If those names aren’t immediately familiar, the music should be.

The guitars were distorted and fuzzy. The drums sounded like they were being played in a basement. Mark Arm’s vocals could shift from sarcastic sneering to full-on screaming without warning.

And there was a willingness to sound completely out of control.

That combination became one of the foundations of the Seattle sound.

Mudhoney’s relationship with Sub Pop was crucial.

The label was still a tiny operation when Mudhoney released their debut single, “Touch Me I’m Sick,” in 1988.

That song became one of the defining recordings of the early Seattle scene.

It was loud, nasty and catchy in exactly the right proportions.

It also demonstrated something important about the bands coming out of Seattle.

They weren’t trying to sound like polished arena-rock stars.

They didn’t seem particularly interested in sounding fashionable either.

Mudhoney sounded like a band that had spent too much time listening to punk and garage records and had decided to make everything louder.

“Touch Me I’m Sick” became a cult classic, and Mudhoney quickly became one of the most recognizable names associated with Sub Pop.

Suddenly Everybody Wanted to Be From Seattle

By the early 1990s, Seattle had become the center of the rock universe.

Record companies were signing anything that had a flannel shirt and a distorted guitar.

Bands that had spent years playing tiny clubs were suddenly being offered major-label contracts.

Nirvana’s changed everything.

Soundgarden broke through.

Alice in Chains became a major rock act.

The term “grunge” was suddenly everywhere.

Mudhoney, however, never became a superstar.

That wasn’t necessarily because they weren’t good enough.

In fact, their refusal to chase mainstream success may have been part of the reason they remained so respected.

They were never particularly interested in cleaning up their sound for radio.

They didn’t suddenly start writing power ballads.

They didn’t reinvent themselves to take advantage of the grunge explosion.

They just kept being Mudhoney.

The Problem With Being Influential

Mudhoney’s biggest historical problem is that they were more influential than commercially successful.

That’s a strange position for a band to occupy.

They helped create the sound.

Other bands became famous for it.

It’s similar to being the person who invents a recipe and then watching somebody else become famous after opening a restaurant serving it.

Mudhoney helped establish the distorted, ugly, sarcastic side of Seattle rock.

But when the rest of the world discovered Seattle, the spotlight landed elsewhere.

They became the cool band’s favorite band.

That’s great for credibility.

It isn’t necessarily great for your Wikipedia page.

They Had More Than One Song

Another reason Mudhoney gets overlooked is that casual listeners often know only “Touch Me I’m Sick.”

That’s a shame because the band’s catalog is much deeper.

Their self-titled 1989 album remains one of the essential documents of the early Sub Pop era.

Then came Every Good Boy Deserves Fudge in 1991, arguably one of their strongest records.

Instead of chasing the increasingly polished alternative-rock sound, Mudhoney doubled down on their weirdness.

There were punk influences, garage-rock riffs, noisy experiments and surprisingly catchy melodies.

They sounded like they didn’t care whether anybody understood what they were doing.

That attitude was increasingly rare as alternative rock became a commercial industry.

They Even Went Major Label

Mudhoney eventually signed with Reprise Records and released in 1992.

For a moment, it looked like the band might finally receive the commercial success that had eluded them.

But the album demonstrated that Mudhoney could make the jump to a major label without completely losing their identity.

They remained gloriously unconcerned with becoming the next Pearl Jam.

Eventually they returned to the independent world and continued recording.

And that’s one of the most impressive things about their story.

They didn’t disappear when grunge faded.

They didn’t become a nostalgia act.

They just kept making records.

The Band That Refused to Go Away

Mudhoney’s longevity is actually one of the reasons they are so easy to overlook.

They’re not a dramatic “what happened to them?” story.

They never broke up for decades.

They never had a spectacular fall from the top.

That isn’t necessarily the kind of story that generates documentaries and endless nostalgia pieces.

But it might be the better story.

Mudhoney survived the grunge explosion, the death of grunge, the rise of alternative rock, the decline of alternative rock, the digital music revolution and the streaming era.

They were still Mudhoney.

Mark Arm’s Voice Remains Instantly Recognizable

One of the band’s greatest assets has always been Mark Arm.

His voice doesn’t sound like a conventional rock singer.

Sometimes it sounds like he’s barely holding the song together.

That was perfect for Mudhoney.

There is no mistaking him once you hear him.

Steve Turner’s guitar work is equally important.

Instead of the polished riffs that would dominate mainstream rock, Mudhoney embraced fuzz, feedback and noise.

The guitars often sound like they’re being pushed beyond their limits.

That’s part of the appeal.

The imperfections become the sound.

Mudhoney still has a loyal fan base.

They still release music.

They remain hugely respected by musicians and serious alternative-rock fans.

But culturally, they have been overshadowed.

The story of grunge has become a story about Nirvana, Pearl Jam, Soundgarden and Alice in Chains.

Mudhoney is often treated as part of the opening chapter rather than one of the main characters.

Because without bands like Mudhoney, the Seattle explosion would have looked very different.

They helped create the environment that made the entire movement possible.

They were there before the major labels came calling.

They were there before the flannel shirts became a fashion statement.

They were there before everybody suddenly claimed to have discovered Seattle.

And they kept going after everybody else moved on.

The Ultimate “Forgotten” Band

Mudhoney isn’t really forgotten.

They’re something more interesting.

Their influence is enormous compared with their mainstream profile.

Their songs still sound filthy and energetic.

Their early records remain essential listening for anyone interested in the origins of grunge.

And their refusal to turn themselves into a polished commercial product is probably one reason their music has aged so well.

If you only know Mudhoney because of “Touch Me I’m Sick,” you’ve barely scratched the surface.

Play Every Good Boy Deserves Fudge.

Then work your way through the later albums.

You’ll find a band that wasn’t simply riding the grunge wave.

They helped create the damn wave.

And maybe that’s the weirdest part of Mudhoney’s legacy.

They were never the biggest band in Seattle.

They were never the richest.

They were never the most famous.

But when the history of alternative rock gets traced back far enough, their fingerprints are all over it.

That’s not being forgotten.

That’s being one of the bands everyone else forgot to thank.

items.title: Humpday Hottie: Dove Cameron
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Dove Cameron is an American actress, singer, and performer who became widely known through her work with Disney Channel before developing a broader career in music, film, and television. Born Chloe Celeste Hosterman in Bainbridge Island, Washington, in 1996, she adopted the professional name Dove Cameron in honor of her late father.

Cameron became a major young television star through the Disney Channel series , which premiered in 2013. The unusual premise allowed her to play both Liv Rooney, an actress returning home, and Liv’s identical twin sister Maddie, an athletic teenager. Cameron’s ability to portray two distinctly different characters helped establish her as one of Disney Channel’s most recognizable performers.

She expanded her audience through the film series, beginning with in 2015. Cameron played Mal, the daughter of Maleficent, and reprised the role in the subsequent films. The franchise became a major part of Disney’s late-2010s youth culture and gave Cameron opportunities to combine acting, singing, and dancing.

Music eventually became an increasingly important part of her career. Her solo work moved away from the Disney sound and toward contemporary pop, with songs exploring relationships, identity, and personal experiences. Her 2022 single “Boyfriend” became an international breakthrough, gaining substantial attention through social media and streaming platforms.

Cameron has also pursued acting outside Disney, appearing in projects including and the film . Her career demonstrates the transition from child and teen television star to a more independent performer working across several areas of entertainment.

With her distinctive voice, versatile acting abilities, and strong connection with younger audiences, Dove Cameron has established herself as a performer whose career extends well beyond the Disney Channel platform that first made her famous.

items.title: Troma Tuesday: Squeeze Play
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are movies that make you think. There are movies that make you laugh. And then there are movies like , where the main challenge is simply accepting that someone actually got all of this into a finished movie.

Released in 1979, is a low-budget sex comedy built around softball, romance, rivalry and enough questionable decision-making to fill several respectable movies. It comes from that wonderful era of exploitation filmmaking when a movie didn’t necessarily need a huge budget, a complicated plot or even particularly convincing acting. It just needed a poster that looked interesting enough to make somebody hand over a few dollars at the theater.

And definitely knows what kind of movie it is.

The basic setup is wonderfully ridiculous. A group of women put together a softball team to take on a men’s team, turning an ordinary recreational game into an excuse for competition, flirting and a whole lot of sexual comedy. The plot is less concerned with realism than with getting everyone onto the field and finding increasingly silly ways to create romantic complications.

It’s basically if someone removed the inspirational speeches, replaced the budget with pocket change and decided that subtlety was an unnecessary expense.

The softball angle is actually one of the movie’s better ideas.

There is something inherently funny about taking a completely ordinary suburban activity and treating it like a life-or-death sporting event. The movie understands that its audience isn’t necessarily here for the finer points of baseball strategy. Nobody is going to be breaking down defensive shifts after watching .

The game is simply an excuse to put a bunch of characters together and let the movie’s various romantic and comedic situations develop.

The movie is very much a product of its time. Its idea of comedy is broad, its sexual humor is unapologetic and its characters are often less like fully developed human beings and more like walking setups for the next joke.

That’s not necessarily a criticism.

Actually, it’s part of the charm.

Movies like weren’t trying to win awards. They were designed for audiences who wanted something light, cheap and a little bit naughty. The whole thing has the unmistakable atmosphere of a movie that could have been discovered on a late-night cable channel years after its original release.

The production itself has that low-budget late-’70s look that makes everything feel slightly more authentic than a polished studio comedy would.

The locations don’t feel glamorous.

The costumes don’t feel expensive.

The characters don’t appear to have unlimited wardrobes.

And nobody seems particularly concerned with making the whole thing look bigger than it is.

That gives a strange charm.

It feels like a movie made by people who knew exactly what they had and weren’t going to waste time pretending otherwise.

The biggest problem is the humor.

Some of it works surprisingly well, especially when the movie leans into the absurdity of the situation. But a lot of the jokes are firmly locked in the late 1970s. What was considered outrageous or hilarious at the time can occasionally feel more awkward than funny today.

The movie also isn’t particularly interested in subtle character development. People fall for each other because the plot needs them to. Rivalries appear because the movie needs a conflict. Romantic complications arrive exactly when the screenplay needs another complication.

You don’t watch because you need to know whether these characters will undergo meaningful personal growth.

You watch because you want to see what ridiculous thing happens next.

That’s an important distinction.

And honestly, there is something refreshing about a movie that doesn’t pretend to be more important than it is.

Modern comedies often feel like they need to have a message. has no such problem.

Its message is basically:

Get a softball team together.

Make everybody attractive.

The movie’s biggest strength is its willingness to embrace its own silliness. It doesn’t have the polish of a major studio production, but it has personality. There is a particular kind of charm that comes from watching a movie made during the period when exploitation films could still find an audience simply by being weird, cheap and entertaining.

also benefits from being short on pretension. It doesn’t ask the viewer to admire its artistry or contemplate the human condition. It just wants to entertain you for a while.

There are stretches where the movie feels repetitive, and some of the comedy hasn’t aged especially well. The pacing can also drag when the movie isn’t actively moving toward another joke or softball-related complication.

But when it hits the right tone, becomes exactly what it should be: a goofy, low-budget snapshot of late-’70s exploitation comedy.

It’s the kind of movie where you can almost imagine the pitch meeting.

“It’s about a women’s softball team.”

“And there are romantic complications.”

That’s basically the entire business plan.

isn’t a lost cinematic masterpiece. It isn’t secretly one of the great sports movies. It isn’t going to make anyone rethink the possibilities of the romantic comedy.

But that’s missing the point.

It’s a movie from an era when filmmakers could make something cheap, silly and mildly outrageous, throw it into theaters and see what happened. That kind of filmmaking has largely disappeared, which makes movies like more interesting today than they probably were when they were released.

It’s occasionally ridiculous.

And it’s exactly the sort of movie that becomes more entertaining when you stop expecting it to be good and simply enjoy it for what it is.

is not a great movie.

But it is a wonderfully goofy example of late-’70s exploitation comedy, and sometimes that’s all you really need. Put it on, don’t expect sophistication, and enjoy the strange little time capsule that emerges from the other side.

items.title: Song Battle: Echo & the Bunnymen – “The Killing Moon” vs. The Church – “Under the Milky Way”
items.author: Schill
items.content:
Two songs. Two bands. Two completely different ways of making atmospheric rock feel enormous.

Echo & the Bunnymen’s “The Killing Moon” and The Church’s “Under the Milky Way” are both defining songs of alternative rock, but they approach atmosphere from opposite directions.

“The Killing Moon” is dark, dramatic and hypnotic. Ian McCulloch’s deep, commanding vocal sits above Will Sergeant’s shimmering guitar work, creating a song that feels mysterious from the very first note.

“Under the Milky Way” is dreamy, spacious and almost otherworldly. Steve Kilbey’s detached vocal floats over layers of guitars, keyboards and atmospheric production, creating something that feels less like a traditional rock song and more like a late-night hallucination.

One feels like midnight in an empty city.

The other feels like staring into the sky at 2 a.m.

Both became signature songs for their bands.

Both remain staples of alternative rock.

Song Profile: “The Killing Moon”

Released in 1984 on Echo & the Bunnymen’s , “The Killing Moon” is one of those songs that seems to exist outside of time.

The opening immediately establishes the mood. Will Sergeant’s guitar work is atmospheric without becoming overly complicated, while the rhythm section gives the song a steady, almost hypnotic pulse.

Then Ian McCulloch enters.

His deep, dramatic voice gives the song a sense of authority. He doesn’t sound like he’s simply singing over the music. He sounds like he’s commanding the entire atmosphere around him.

The arrangement is remarkably restrained considering how dramatic the song feels. Strings add another layer of tension, while the guitars shimmer around the edges.

“The Killing Moon” builds its impact through mood, melody and sheer presence.

It is dark without being depressing, romantic without becoming sentimental and mysterious without losing its hook.

That combination is incredibly difficult to pull off.

Song Profile: “Under the Milky Way”

The Church released “Under the Milky Way” in 1988 on , and it became the band’s defining song.

Steve Kilbey’s vocal performance is the opposite of Ian McCulloch’s.

Where McCulloch sounds commanding, Kilbey sounds distant and almost detached, as if he’s observing everything from somewhere far away.

The song’s instrumentation creates the perfect environment for that vocal.

The guitars shimmer, the rhythm section remains understated and the production gives everything plenty of space.

One of the song’s most distinctive elements is the atmospheric keyboard work, which adds an almost otherworldly quality to the arrangement.

The result is a song that feels enormous without ever becoming loud.

“Under the Milky Way” doesn’t demand attention.

It simply creates a world and lets you wander around inside it.

“The Killing Moon” is beautifully constructed.

The melody is strong, the verses build tension and the chorus provides a memorable release without destroying the song’s mysterious mood.

“Under the Milky Way” is equally sophisticated, but its strength lies more in atmosphere and arrangement than in traditional song structure.

Both songs are deceptively simple.

But “The Killing Moon” has a slightly stronger sense of dramatic progression.

Echo & the Bunnymen take the opening round.

This is a fascinating contrast.

Ian McCulloch possesses one of alternative rock’s most distinctive voices. His baritone is deep, dramatic and immediately recognizable.

Steve Kilbey’s vocal is almost the complete opposite. His delivery on “Under the Milky Way” is cool, detached and slightly hypnotic.

McCulloch sounds like he’s standing directly in front of you.

Kilbey sounds like he’s somewhere in the distance.

Both approaches work perfectly.

But McCulloch’s voice gives “The Killing Moon” a greater sense of personality.

Will Sergeant’s guitar playing is one of the great strengths of “The Killing Moon.”

He doesn’t simply provide chords. His playing creates an atmosphere around the vocal, with shimmering tones that give the song its unmistakable character.

The Church have an equally impressive guitar sound.

“Under the Milky Way” uses layered guitars to create a huge amount of space. The parts aren’t necessarily flashy, but they are essential to the song’s mood.

This is one of those rounds where technical complexity isn’t really the point.

The question is which guitar work creates the stronger identity.

Sergeant’s playing is simply more immediately recognizable.

This may be the most difficult round to judge.

“The Killing Moon” sounds dark, mysterious and slightly dangerous. It has a cinematic quality that makes the song feel larger than its actual running time.

“Under the Milky Way” goes in the opposite direction.

The guitars, keyboards and spacious production create the sensation of floating through the night.

If “The Killing Moon” is walking through a dark city street at midnight, “Under the Milky Way” is lying on the hood of a car staring at the stars.

Both create extraordinary atmospheres.

But The Church have an advantage here.

Winner: Under the Milky Way

The Church win the atmosphere battle by creating an almost dreamlike environment.

“The Killing Moon” has a chorus that feels dramatic and powerful without suddenly becoming a completely different song.

McCulloch’s vocal rises while the instrumentation expands around him.

“Under the Milky Way” takes a subtler approach.

Its chorus is memorable because of the melody and the way the entire arrangement opens up around Kilbey’s vocal.

But it doesn’t have quite the same immediate impact.

Echo & the Bunnymen get another point.

This is where “Under the Milky Way” becomes extremely difficult to beat.

The production on the song gives every element room to breathe. The guitars, keyboards, vocals and rhythm section occupy their own spaces without making the track feel cluttered.

The sound is polished without becoming sterile.

“The Killing Moon” has a fantastic production as well, particularly considering how much atmosphere is created from relatively few ingredients.

But The Church’s recording feels almost perfectly designed for headphones.

You can hear something different every time you listen.

Winner: Under the Milky Way

The Church take the production round.

Both songs have instantly recognizable openings.

“The Killing Moon” announces itself within seconds. That guitar sound and McCulloch’s entrance are unmistakable.

“Under the Milky Way” has the same advantage. The opening atmosphere and Kilbey’s voice immediately establish the song.

But there is a difference between recognizing a song and remembering its melody.

“The Killing Moon” has a chorus that tends to stick around in your head.

Echo & the Bunnymen win on pure musical recall.

“The Killing Moon” became one of the defining songs of the post-punk era and helped cement Echo & the Bunnymen as one of the most important British alternative bands of the 1980s.

Its continued presence in movies, television and alternative-rock culture has kept the song remarkably recognizable decades after its release.

“Under the Milky Way” had a similar effect for The Church.

The song became a major international hit and introduced the Australian band to an audience far beyond the post-punk and alternative scenes they had occupied previously.

Both songs became definitive recordings for their respective bands.

But “The Killing Moon” has arguably had the longer cultural afterlife.

The Bunnymen take another close round.

This is where “Under the Milky Way” makes a serious comeback.

“The Killing Moon” is one of those songs that demands attention. Its dramatic structure and powerful vocal performance make it incredibly rewarding, but it’s also a fairly intense experience.

“Under the Milky Way” is different.

You can put it on late at night and simply let it exist in the background.

Then you can listen to it again with headphones and suddenly notice another guitar texture or keyboard layer.

It’s the kind of song that changes depending on the mood you’re in.

Winner: Under the Milky Way

The Church win because the song seems to reveal more of itself with repeated listening.

Round 10: Overall Alternative Rock Factor

This final round comes down to what you want alternative rock to be.

“The Killing Moon” represents the dramatic side of the genre.

It is mysterious, emotional, guitar-driven and unmistakably British. It takes post-punk’s darker tendencies and turns them into something almost cinematic.

“Under the Milky Way” represents the more atmospheric side.

It’s less interested in aggression and more interested in creating a mood. It feels spacious, slightly strange and completely comfortable existing somewhere between rock, psychedelia and dream pop.

“The Killing Moon” is the more powerful song.

“Under the Milky Way” is the more immersive song.

And when considering the overall identity of alternative rock, that immersive quality gives The Church the edge.

Winner: Under the Milky Way

The Killing Moon — 6 rounds

Under the Milky Way — 4 rounds

The Winner: “The Killing Moon”

Echo & the Bunnymen take the battle, but this is much closer than the final score suggests.

“The Killing Moon” has almost everything you could want from an alternative-rock classic. The guitar work is instantly recognizable, Ian McCulloch has one of the most distinctive voices of the era, and the song manages to sound both intimate and enormous.

But “Under the Milky Way” is an extraordinary piece of atmospheric songwriting.

The Church understood that sometimes the spaces between the instruments can be just as important as the instruments themselves. Steve Kilbey’s detached vocal, the shimmering guitars and the spacious production create a song that feels completely removed from ordinary reality.

It is difficult to imagine either song being performed by the other band.

That may be the greatest compliment you can give both.

Echo & the Bunnymen made darkness sound romantic.

The Church made the night sound endless.

“The Killing Moon” is the song you put on when you want to feel something.

“Under the Milky Way” is the song you put on when you want to disappear for a while.

But when the two go head-to-head, Echo & the Bunnymen’s combination of songwriting, vocals, guitar work and sheer dramatic presence gives them the victory.

Winner: Echo & the Bunnymen — “The Killing Moon”

items.title: Satudys 80s Jam: Cher – If I Could Turn Back Time
items.author: Schill
items.content:
By the time Cher released “If I Could Turn Back Time” in 1989, she had already lived several careers in one lifetime. She had been a folk-pop star with Sonny Bono, a television personality, a movie actress, a disco singer, and a successful solo artist. But somehow, at 43 years old, Cher was about to have one of the biggest hits of her career.

Released on her album , “If I Could Turn Back Time” became one of Cher’s signature songs and one of the most memorable power ballads of the late 1980s.

The song was written by Diane Warren, who had become one of the era’s most successful songwriters. Warren specialized in enormous emotional pop songs, and “If I Could Turn Back Time” fit perfectly into that tradition. Its subject was simple: regret over a damaged relationship and the desperate wish to go back and fix what went wrong.

Cher was an ideal singer for it.

Her voice had always possessed a distinctive combination of strength and vulnerability. She didn’t need to oversell the emotion. The slightly husky quality of her voice made the song sound like it was coming from someone who had actually lived through the regrets she was singing about.

The production, however, made it unmistakably 1989.

Big drums, synthesizers, layered backing vocals, dramatic guitar, and an increasingly enormous arrangement transformed the song from a relatively straightforward ballad into a full-scale pop-rock production. Everything builds toward the chorus, where Cher’s vocal becomes the emotional center of the recording.

Then came the music video.

And that is where “If I Could Turn Back Time” became permanently attached to 1980s pop culture.

The video was filmed aboard the USS and featured Cher performing for sailors. She wore a black, highly revealing outfit that became almost as famous as the song itself. The video generated controversy and received restrictions on some television outlets, but it also made Cher impossible to ignore.

The outfit became an enduring piece of pop-culture history, while the video itself became one of the defining visual moments of late-1980s MTV.

Ironically, all the attention surrounding the video could have overshadowed the song.

“If I Could Turn Back Time” became a major international hit, reaching the top 10 in several countries and becoming one of Cher’s most recognizable recordings. In the United States, it reached number three on the Billboard Hot 100.

The song also demonstrated something remarkable about Cher’s career: she wasn’t simply surviving into a new decade. She was successfully adapting to it.

The 1980s had been full of musical reinvention. Artists who had been successful in earlier decades had to figure out how to compete in a world dominated by MTV, synthesizers, enormous productions, and increasingly image-conscious pop.

Cher understood the assignment.

By the end of the decade, she had transformed herself once again.

What makes “If I Could Turn Back Time” endure isn’t simply its gigantic chorus or unforgettable music video. It’s the emotion at the heart of the song. Regret is universal. Everyone has something they wish they could redo, something they wish they had said differently, or some moment they wish they could revisit.

Cher takes that very familiar feeling and turns it into a huge piece of late-1980s pop.

And the fact that she was already a veteran performer when the song became a hit makes the achievement even more impressive.

“If I Could Turn Back Time” wasn’t the beginning of Cher’s career.

It was another reinvention.

She had already been famous for decades, but in 1989 she managed to become something else again: an MTV-era pop superstar with one of the decade’s most recognizable songs and videos.

The song may be about wanting to reverse the past.

Cher, however, was doing the opposite.

She was moving forward—and proving that she wasn’t anywhere near finished yet.

items.title: Forgotten Band: The Muffs
items.author: Schill
items.content:
There are bands that disappear because they were terrible. There are bands that disappear because they had one hit and nothing else. And then there are bands like The Muffs, who somehow managed to release a stack of excellent records, build a devoted following, influence plenty of musicians, and still end up in the musical equivalent of a forgotten drawer.

The Muffs were never completely unknown. Alternative-rock fans who were paying attention in the 1990s knew exactly who they were. Their music appeared in movies, television shows and video games, and their version of “Kids in America” introduced them to an even larger audience.

But compared with the amount of talent in the band, The Muffs should have been much bigger.

They were loud, catchy, funny, messy and completely uninterested in pretending to be cooler than they actually were. They could sound like a punk band one minute and a ridiculously infectious power-pop band the next. At the center of it all was Kim Shattuck, whose voice could go from sweet to ferocious in the space of about three seconds.

And that’s probably the best way to describe The Muffs.

They sounded like they were having fun.

From The Pandoras to The Muffs

The story of The Muffs starts with Kim Shattuck and Melanie Vammen, who had previously been members of the Los Angeles garage-rock group The Pandoras.

After leaving The Pandoras, Shattuck and Vammen formed The Muffs in the early 1990s. Ronnie Barnett of The Muffs’ eventual classic lineup joined on bass, while Roy McDonald became the drummer.

The band quickly developed a sound that was impossible to mistake.

There were punk influences everywhere, but The Muffs weren’t interested in making relentlessly aggressive music. They understood the value of a great melody.

Their songs were short, loud and packed with hooks.

That combination helped separate them from many of the alternative and punk bands around them.

They could be abrasive without becoming exhausting.

They could be poppy without becoming manufactured.

And they had something else that a lot of bands lacked:

The band’s self-titled debut arrived in 1993.

It immediately established what The Muffs were all about.

The songs were fast, distorted and catchy, with Shattuck’s vocals constantly bouncing between melodic singing and her trademark screaming.

That scream became one of the band’s defining characteristics.

It wasn’t the polished, carefully controlled kind of screaming that eventually became common in alternative rock. Shattuck sounded like she might actually lose her voice halfway through the song.

That unpredictability was part of the appeal.

You never quite knew when a sweet pop melody was about to explode into a furious yell.

The Muffs followed the debut with in 1995, which remains one of their essential albums.

If the first album established their sound, demonstrated just how good they could be at writing ridiculously memorable songs.

Tracks like “Sad Tomorrow” and “Oh Nina” showed that underneath all the distortion and attitude was a genuinely gifted pop songwriter.

Then Came “Kids in America”

The Muffs’ biggest exposure came when they recorded their own version of Kim Wilde’s “Kids in America.”

Their version appeared on the soundtrack to the 1995 movie .

Suddenly, a band that had been operating in the alternative underground was being heard by a much larger audience.

The song fit perfectly with the movie’s energetic teenage aesthetic.

And it sounded unmistakably like The Muffs.

For a moment, it seemed like the band might finally break into the mainstream.

But that’s where the story takes a familiar turn.

The Muffs never became massive.

They never became one of the defining bands of the decade.

They remained a cult favorite.

And, in hindsight, that may have been both a blessing and a curse.

The Problem With Being Too Good for the Mainstream

The Muffs occupied an awkward musical space.

They were too punk for mainstream pop.

Too melodic for hardcore.

Too scrappy for polished alternative rock.

Too weird to be packaged neatly.

And yet they had the songwriting ability to produce genuine pop hits.

That combination should have made them huge.

Instead, it made them difficult to categorize.

The 1990s music industry loved categories.

The Muffs didn’t fit perfectly into any of them.

They simply sounded like The Muffs.

That is usually great for artistic longevity.

It isn’t always great for selling millions of records.

They Never Really Went Away

The Muffs continued recording throughout the 1990s and 2000s, releasing albums including , Alert Today, Alive Tomorrow, and .

They never completely disappeared.

They just became one of those bands that you had to know about.

If you were digging through alternative-rock playlists or looking for great punk-pop records, eventually you would stumble across them.

And when you did, there was usually the same reaction:

“Why didn’t I listen to these guys earlier?”

That’s one of the strange things about The Muffs.

Their music hasn’t aged particularly badly.

In fact, some of it sounds better now.

The production might sound unmistakably 1990s, but the songs themselves are timeless little blasts of power pop.

They don’t require nostalgia to work.

They’re simply good songs.

Kim Shattuck Was the Secret Weapon

It’s impossible to discuss The Muffs without talking about Kim Shattuck.

She wasn’t simply the singer.

She was the personality of the band.

Her voice could be sarcastic, vulnerable, hilarious, furious and sweet, sometimes within the same song.

She also had an instinct for keeping songs from becoming overly polished.

The imperfections were part of the charm.

Shattuck later became a member of The Pixies for a short period and also continued performing with The Muffs.

Her death in 2019 at the age of 56 was a devastating loss for fans of the band and the wider punk and alternative community.

The Muffs continued after her death through archival material and releases, but there was obviously no replacing the person who had given the band its unmistakable personality.

Why Did We Forget The Muffs?

A memorable soundtrack appearance.

And enough albums to build a substantial catalog.

They simply never became part of the standard story of 1990s alternative rock.

Mention Nirvana, Green Day, The Offspring, Weezer or Hole and most people immediately know what you’re talking about.

Mention The Muffs and you might get:

“The Muffs… wait. I know that name.”

Then you play “Kids in America.”

A band you forgot you loved.

The good news is that The Muffs are incredibly easy to rediscover.

Start with and . Then work through the later records.

You’ll quickly discover that “Kids in America” isn’t some isolated novelty.

It’s just the song that happened to escape the cult.

The real appeal of The Muffs is the combination of melody and chaos.

They could write a gorgeous pop song and then scream their heads off in the middle of it.

They could sound polished for thirty seconds before deliberately blowing the whole thing apart.

They were punk without being miserable.

They were pop without being fake.

And they were funny without turning every song into a joke.

That’s a pretty difficult balance to pull off.

The Muffs deserved a much bigger place in the history of 1990s alternative music.

They weren’t just a soundtrack band.

They weren’t just another punk-pop group.

They were one of the most consistently entertaining bands of their era.

And if you’ve forgotten them, don’t feel too bad.

That’s basically the story of The Muffs.

They’ve been waiting patiently for you to remember.

And once you do, you’re probably going to wonder how the hell you forgot them in the first place.
